title: I neither know nor think that I know
author: Plato
lines: Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows
anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—
for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows;
I neither know nor think that I know.
I seem to have slightly the advantage of him.
why: The real words behind 'I know that I know nothing'. Socrates has just questioned a politician who was thought wise, and found he was not. His only advantage was this: he did not think he knew what he did not know. Say it when you are tempted to sound surer than you are.

title: Deep water
author: Proverbs
lines: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water,
but a man of understanding will draw it out.
why: Two lines on what a good teacher, friend or parent does: not pouring wisdom in, but drawing out what is already in a person, as Socrates did with his questions. Say it before a conversation where you are tempted to give advice instead of listening.

title: Not evil for evil
author: Plato
lines: Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to any one,
whatever evil we may have suffered from him.
neither injury nor retaliation nor warding off evil by evil is ever right.
why: In prison, as his friend urged him to escape, Socrates laid down the principle on which he would decide: never return wrong for wrong, even to a city that has wronged you. Four centuries later Paul wrote, 'Repay no one evil for evil' (Romans 12:17). Say it when you want to get even.
